newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Australian leader pledges close Indonesian ties.
newsitem.headline: Australian leader pledges close Indonesian ties.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard told President Suharto on Monday that his country's relationship with Indonesia was of the greatest significance.

Speaking at a state dinner on his first official visit to Indonesia since taking office six months ago, Howard said he wanted to reaffirm personally to Suharto the commitment of his conservative government to the relationship.
"This relationship is of the very greatest significance to Australia and brings substantial benefits to our region as a whole," Howard said in his speech.

His comments echoed those by his Labor predecessor Paul Keating, regarded as having a special relationship with Suharto, who in March 1994 said: "No country is more important to Australia than Indonesia."
Howard, who arrived in Jakarta earlier on Monday, was welcomed by the Indonesian leader at Freedom Palace, where he was greeted by an artillery salute booming out across the city.
The Australian leader later paid a visit to the Kalibata Heroes Cemetery and made a courtesy call on Vice-President Try
While relations between the two neighbours have been rocky at times, Howard's visit is seen as boosting ties and emphasising his government's commitment to Asia.

"We have to recognise that each country brings different strengths to the relationship. We should acknowledge each other's achievements. We should not presume to have the answers to each other's problems," Howard said.

"We are very different and we cannot expect to see eye to eye. No country can be asked to deny its history, principles or culture. But when disagreements emerge, they should be seen in the context of the overriding mutual interests we share and the immense benefit of a close relationship between us," he added.
Suharto said in his address to the dinner differences would not hinder bilateral relations but he warned against nations interfering in the domestic affairs of other nations.
Addressing the issue of human rights, Suharto said the rights such as freedom of speech could not be separated from economic, educational and social rights.

"This does not mean mean that civil and political rights must be put in second place because ecomomic, social and cultural as well as civil and political rights are integrated and cannot be separated," Suharto said.
"Economic and political development must go ahead hand in hand and be mutually support," he said.
Indonesia's human rights record, particularly in East Timor, has been the subject of continued vocal criticism by activists, churches and some politicians in Australia.
Deputy Prime Minister and Trade Minister Tim Fischer said in Jakarta last week that Howard's visit was a "reflection of the dynamic relationship between Australia and Indonesia".
It was also about "further building the economic linkage" between the two countries, Fischer added.
Indonesia is Australia's 12th largest trading partner and one of its fastest growing markets. Howard said two-way trade in 1995-96 was worth A$4.2 billion ($3.3 billion).
Howard will have further talks with Suharto on Tuesday and leaves for Japan early on Wednesday. His two-nation visit had earlier been postponed after his wife fell ill. (A$1 = US$0.79)
